operation_details.item: The user uses Google Fonts as one of their type sources.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I'm reviewing the licensing notes for the rebrand package before I hand it off to the developer.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Good idea. How do you usually handle type licensing for client work?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I use Adobe Fonts for most client work.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That's convenient since Adobe Fonts is bundled with Creative Cloud. What about when a project needs a more distinctive look?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I buy direct foundry licenses for display faces.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Got it. Do you keep a central record so you know which fonts are cleared for which client?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: All client typefaces are logged in the license tracker.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: That must make audits and handoffs much easier.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: I use Google Fonts as one of my type sources.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Right, Google Fonts is useful for open-source options that keep the project lightweight.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Exactly. I like having that option for less-brand-critical pieces.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Sounds like a solid mix: Adobe Fonts for most work, direct foundry licenses for display faces, Google Fonts for open-source needs, and everything tracked in the license tracker.
